title: Split the Team Between Two Offices
statement:
A company is flying 2n people to an offsite that runs in two offices, A and B. costs[i] = [a, b] means person i costs a to send to office A and b to send to office B.

Exactly n people must go to each office. Return the minimum total cost.

examples.why: Persons 0 and 2 go to A (10 + 50), persons 1 and 3 go to B (20 + 30).

Everyone is cheaper at A, but only two may go there. Send the two who would lose the most by switching: person 3 (saves 70) and person 0 (saves 45). 30 + 5 + 30 + 25 = 90. Picking the two cheapest A tickets would cost 140.
One each: person 1 to A for 4, person 0 to B for 3.

hints: Start by sending everyone to A. Now exactly n people must switch to B. What does each switch cost?
Switching person i from A to B changes the total by b − a. You want the n switches with the smallest change.
Sort people by a − b. The first half (most to gain from A) go to A, the rest to B.

explain.intuition:
Picking the cheaper office for each person fails as soon as too many prefer the same one. The useful number is not the price but the difference: how much extra a person costs if sent to their worse office.

Imagine everyone booked for A first. You must move exactly n people to B, and moving person i changes the bill by b − a. To keep the bill low, move the n people with the smallest b − a, which is the same as keeping in A the n people with the smallest a − b. A sort by a − b puts them in order. Swapping any A person with any B person from the sorted halves can only raise the cost, which is why the greedy choice is safe.
steps: Send the first n people to A: add their a.
Send the last n people to B: add their b.
pitfalls: Sending each person to their cheaper office and then patching the counts. It breaks when most people prefer one side, as in the second example.
Sorting by a alone, or by min(a, b). The cheapest A ticket may belong to someone whose B ticket is just as cheap.
Forgetting that the split must be exactly n and n, not "at most n".

solutions.title: DP over people and A-count
solutions.idea: best[j] = minimum cost with j of the people so far sent to A. Each new person either goes to A (j grows) or to B.

solutions.title: Sort by the price difference
solutions.idea: Order people by how much cheaper A is for them. The first half go to A, the second half to B.

followups: There are three offices and each must get exactly a third of the people. Does a single sort still work?
Office A can take between n − k and n + k people. How does the greedy change?
